description: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
description: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.

title: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease
description: After more than 35 years of research, scientists have uncovered surprising clues about what really drives Lyme disease risk. Contrary to longstanding assumptions, deer populations appear less important than mice, which can fuel a 40% increase in tick numbers the following year. Even acorn production can predict tick population surges two years in advance, while extreme temperatures may be far less deadly to ticks than scientists once believed.

description:

Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific.
The eggs incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach after the historic discovery of two separate nests in September at southern California beaches, a shift likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions.

title: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
description: Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.

title: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought
description: Scientists have discovered that the heart ages unevenly, with surprising hotspots of inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than the heart muscle. The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about cardiac aging and could help researchers develop new ways to protect the heart as we grow older.

title: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
description: MIT scientists discovered that carefully timed bursts of gentle pink noise during sleep can strengthen the brain’s natural cleaning waves, which help flush away potentially harmful waste. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments aimed at improving sleep and memory while potentially reducing the buildup of proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease.

description: People installing their own solar panels has helped boost the solar share of Pakistan's electricity from 1% to 28%.

title: New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors
description: A major breakthrough in superconductivity research has revealed that one of the essential ingredients for electricity to flow without resistance can exist at room temperature. Scientists discovered that electrons can form stable pairs at much higher temperatures than previously understood, suggesting that a different obstacle may be preventing room-temperature superconductivity.

title: Working in Cape Cod’s waters, he saw an unusual clam. It was the start of an invasion
description:
The unfamiliar mollusk first turned up in this harvester’s haul in 2023. He asked a scientist to identify it, and together they realized they were seeing a potentially harmful, non-native species

Send us your climate questions for the next Stateside guest: Bill McKibben

Shellfish harvester Ernie Eldredge is on the hunt for clams, ankle-deep in water amid a landscape that’s almost desert-like in the wake of the receding tide. He runs his rake through fine white sand again and again without hearing the faint “clink” of its tines hitting a shell.
Eldredge just shrugs and moves on to the next spot. These tidal flats, perched on the elbow of Cape Cod in Chatham, Massachusetts, are constantly changing. Recent fall winds have carried a lot more sand into the area, and Eldredge thinks the clams he was finding over the summer may have moved on.

title: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why
description: Scientists may have finally explained why up to more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from rocks around the world. New research suggests that powerful currents deep inside the planet slowly raised and lowered entire continents, allowing erosion to erase vast stretches of geological history before they were buried and preserved.

title: The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse
description: The massive solar storm that illuminated skies worldwide in May 2024 has uncovered an unexpected twist: Earth's own atmosphere may have helped make the storm so powerful. Satellite measurements revealed that roughly 85% of the charged particles fueling the disturbance originated from Earth's upper atmosphere rather than the solar wind. Scientists also detected an extraordinary 40% weakening of Earth's magnetic field high above the planet.

title: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets
description: Researchers have discovered that a familiar tropical butterfly actually belongs to three nearly identical species, including one previously unknown to science. Hidden ultraviolet wing patterns and DNA differences revealed the truth, leaving scientists puzzled about how the butterflies remain genetically separate despite living side by side.

title: 128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history
description: Ancient ice discovered high in Tibet may be more than 128,000 years old, preserving an extraordinary record of Earth's climate that scientists previously thought had been lost. The discovery reveals a rare glimpse into the last ice age and could reshape our understanding of how glaciers survive dramatic changes in global climate.

title: Why obesity affects men and women differently may be hiding in their fat
description: Scientists at the University of California, Riverside have uncovered a surprising reason why males and females may respond differently to obesity. In a study involving mice, researchers discovered that immune cells traditionally associated with allergies and asthma can either protect against obesity-related inflammation or contribute to harmful metabolic changes, depending on their type and biological sex.

title: Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment
description: Scientists have developed a new technique that uses magnetic nanoparticles to stimulate deep brain regions, dramatically improving Parkinson’s-like movement problems in mice without permanently implanted electrodes. The breakthrough could pave the way for less invasive treatments using injectable particles and wearable magnetic headbands.

title: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s
description: Scientists have uncovered a powerful natural defense against Alzheimer’s disease that could open the door to new treatments. By boosting a protein called SORLA, researchers significantly reduced toxic tau tangles, protected connections between brain cells, and prevented some of the brain shrinkage associated with neurodegeneration in mice. Removing the protein made the damage worse, highlighting its critical protective role.

title: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
description: MIT researchers have discovered that the brain’s natural waste-removal system becomes significantly less effective during sleep as people age. The decline is linked to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and changes in blood flow, potentially offering new clues about why aging increases the risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementia. Surprisingly, some older adults retain the same powerful cleansing waves seen in younger people.

title: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study
description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising genetic connection to spinal degeneration and found that an existing osteoporosis drug can prevent damaging mineral buildup in zebrafish spines. The discovery could pave the way for new treatments that slow or prevent a major cause of chronic back pain.

title: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
description: Stanford researchers have discovered that children who struggle persistently with math may have underlying differences in how their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia were slower to switch strategies, less responsive to changes in difficulty, and less able to improve their approach over time. Distinct patterns of brain activity were linked to these difficulties and could even predict certain math-related abilities.

title: First observation of a giant star swallowing its neighbour
A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret
description: Researchers at the University of Osaka have discovered a remarkable quantum state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. They observed electrons behaving as though they were unusually heavy, including a previously unseen state created by interactions between the ultrathin layer and the copper beneath it. This first-of-its-kind observation reveals a promising new way to control exotic quantum behavior.

title: NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base
description: NASA is offering $1 million in its new Moon Base Challenge, inviting U.S. students to develop innovative solutions for building humanity’s first permanent lunar outpost. From power systems to astronaut safety, their ideas could help make long-term life on the Moon possible and pave the way to Mars.

title: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom
description: Scientists have unexpectedly discovered how to control the magnetic spin inside a single atom's nucleus using radio waves, overturning previous assumptions about atomic behavior. The breakthrough could pave the way for more reliable quantum memory, although researchers are still trying to understand why it works.

title: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian
description: A bizarre, heavily armored amphibian roamed the oceans 237 million years ago, despite the fact that modern amphibians cannot survive entirely in saltwater. Discovered in China, the giant salamander-sized creature may be the first known amphibian to have adapted to a fully marine existence.

title: Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought
description: Scientists have discovered that the first animals to venture onto land nearly 380 million years ago had surprisingly stiff necks, overturning a long-standing theory about evolution. Rather than evolving to help animals turn their heads, necks may have emerged as part of the anatomical changes that allowed them to move using their front limbs.

title: Paleontologists discover “one-in-a-million” fossil with 450-million-year-old soft tissue
description: Scientists have discovered a remarkably preserved 450-million-year-old fossil containing soft tissues from an ancient starfish relative, revealing unexpected details about marine life more than 200 million years before dinosaurs existed. Found in a museum collection, the extraordinarily rare specimen offers new clues about how Earth's earliest reef animals fed, survived, and evolved.

title: ‘Huge experiment in biogeography’: US offshore windfarms are creating artificial reefs
description:
Scientists and fishers study how these ‘reefs’ and the creatures living on them are transforming the ocean floor – and what it means for the fishing industry
A few years ago, Tony DiLernia, a New York-based charter boat captain, heard rumors of prime fishing near the Block Island windfarm, off the tip of Long Island. So he went with his family to see for himself. Almost immediately after motoring up to one of the project’s five turbines, black sea bass and summer flounder started nibbling at his rod and reel.
DiLernia, who has fished for 50 years, wasn’t surprised: he knew about the reef effect, where certain species cluster around structures like the turbines. “It’s what we call ‘stupid fishing’,” he joked. “You’ve got this thousand-foot [signpost] sticking up out of the water saying: ‘Fish here.’”

description:

The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, her ministers and Natural England are breaking the law by failing to intervene to slow the “deeply concerning” decline of Britain’s wild birds, the UK’s environment regulator has said.
New data shows that wild bird populations have dropped to their lowest level on record, with almost half – 45% – of 132 native breeding species in decline over a five-year period.

title: Cop31 as it happened: rich world offering ‘crumbs’ to help poor countries adapt to climate breakdown, campaigners say
description:
Wealthy polluters promised to put $50m into an adaptation fund this week, less than half of what countries promised at last year’s climate summit
California Governor Gavin Newsom was a big presence in Antalya last week, serving as the head of a US delegation that attended unofficially due to President Donald Trump’s withdrawal from the international summit.
Widely seen as a top presidential contender for 2028, Newsom’s strong rhetoric in support of a fossil fuel phase out and other top climate priorities inspired hope that there’s a future for the US – the world’s second biggest emitter – in negotiations. That of course, depends on who ends up as the next resident of the White House, but Newsom made big promises regardless, as the head of California – the world’s fourth largest economy.

title: 125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert
description: A remarkable 125,000-year-old discovery in Saudi Arabia reveals that early humans once thrived beside enormous lakes filled with wildlife in what is now a vast desert. Thousands of stone tools and ancient plant remains suggest these prehistoric people used sophisticated hunting techniques, potentially including weapons enhanced with poisonous plant compounds.

title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
description: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.

title: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago
description: Dinosaurs may have been snacking on seaweed and other ocean foods more than 100 million years ago, according to surprising new evidence hidden in their fossilized teeth. Researchers discovered chemical signatures suggesting that coastal dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals relied partly on nutrients originating in the sea. The findings reveal that marine resources traveled through ancient food chains, supplementing the diets of everything from plant-eating dinosaurs to predators.

title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
description: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.

title: Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains
description: Why do some volcanoes erupt with spectacular lava fountains while others release lava more quietly? Scientists have discovered that a hidden effect of extreme heat inside magma may help explain the difference. Experiments revealed that superheated magma can delay crystal formation for more than eight hours, compared with just 20 minutes in magma that has not been superheated.

title: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
description: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.

title: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago
description: Scientists have uncovered fossils of a giant rodent that lived in Thailand 34 million years ago, revealing that enormous rodents evolved much earlier than previously thought. Named Yakamys sirindhornae, the ancient animal may have weighed around 66 pounds, roughly twice as much as other known rodents of its time.

title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
description: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

title: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.
description: Scientists discovered that although people with and without autism show surprisingly similar average brain activity, individuals with autism exhibit much greater differences from one another, especially in regions involved in social understanding. The findings suggest that traditional research methods may be overlooking crucial differences that could help unlock more personalized autism support.

title: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain
description: New research reveals that biological sex, genetics, and menopause may dramatically influence Alzheimer's risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. Scientists also uncovered surprising differences in immune activity and gut-brain interactions, opening the door to more personalized treatments for neurological disorders.

title: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds
description: Scientists have discovered that vitamin C may help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming in the stomach after eating foods containing nitrates and nitrites. A new mathematical model suggests that taking vitamin C after meals could reduce these harmful reactions, offering a possible new strategy for lowering cancer risk.

title: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected
description: Scientists have discovered that psychopathic traits are associated with surprisingly different patterns of language, with some individuals using more positive words and others expressing greater negativity or less anxiety. The findings challenge familiar stereotypes about psychopathy and suggest that the stories people tell about their lives may offer important clues about their personalities.

title: Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable
description: Smiling may not always make you happier, and new research suggests that forcing yourself to smile repeatedly could actually make you feel worse. In a University of Florida study involving more than 1,100 participants, researchers discovered that while a single artificial smile can provide a small mood boost, repeatedly faking smiles can erase that benefit or even reverse it.

description: The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.

description: The Tees Rivers Trust has been searching for eels to tag and track as they migrate out to sea.
